lessons.title: What Is a Currency War? Defining Competitive Devaluation

body.text: A currency war is not a currency simply getting weaker. It is a central bank deliberately pushing its own currency down to gain a trade edge, and every other affected country deciding how to respond. Confuse a currency war with ordinary depreciation and you will misread every headline in this course.

children.text: Three Words the Financial Press Uses Interchangeably

Depreciation, devaluation and currency war get thrown around as synonyms on business television. For a fund manager or a macro analyst, that sloppiness is expensive. Each term describes a different mechanism, a different motive, and a different signal for positioning. This lesson pins down the definitions before the rest of the course builds on them.

markDefs.definition: A currency losing value against other currencies because of market forces such as trade flows, capital flows or interest rate differentials, with no deliberate policy action behind it.

children.text: Start with
depreciation

. This is what happens to the rupee on an ordinary week: a wider trade deficit, a bout of FII selling on the NSE, a spike in crude oil prices, and the rupee drifts weaker against the dollar without anyone at Mint Street planning it that way. The RBI still shows up in the forex market on days like this, but to smooth the pace of the move, not to engineer a particular level.

markDefs.definition: A central bank or government deliberately weakening its currency, through rate cuts, direct intervention or a policy announcement, specifically to make exports cheaper or to fight domestic deflation.

children.text: Set that against
competitive devaluation

. Here a central bank makes an explicit choice: cut rates further than the domestic situation requires, intervene directly to cap the currency, or announce a new reference level, specifically to make its exports cheaper or to fight deflation at home. The move is intentional, it is usually sudden, and it is aimed at a competitive outcome against other trading nations.

markDefs.definition: A situation where multiple countries treat their exchange rates as competitive tools, each devaluing or intervening in response to the others, rather than letting currencies float on economic fundamentals alone.

children.text: A
currency war

is what you get when competitive devaluation stops being a one-off move and becomes a pattern: one economy devalues, its trading partners feel the pinch on their own exporters, and some of them respond in kind. Nobody has to fire a shot for the label to stick. The term describes a standoff over exchange rates, not a literal conflict.

body.title: Quick Check: Is This a Currency War?
body.question: The rupee weakens from ₹82 to ₹85 against the dollar over three months, driven mainly by FII outflows and a widening current account deficit. The RBI sells dollars on a few sharp days purely to slow the fall, without defending any specific level. Is this competitive devaluation?
options: Yes, because the currency became meaningfully weaker
No, because there was no deliberate policy action aimed at a competitive outcome
Yes, because the RBI intervened in the forex market
No, because the rupee is a fully floating currency with no RBI involvement at all
body.explanation: This is ordinary market depreciation. The RBI's intervention here targets volatility, not a level or a competitive goal, which is exactly the managed float the RBI runs day to day. Option C is wrong because intervention by itself doesn't make a move a devaluation. Option D is wrong because the RBI does intervene routinely, it simply isn't targeting a rate.

children.text: Why Would Any Country Deliberately Weaken Its Own Currency?

Three motives show up again and again across the case studies later in this course. A weaker currency makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers, giving domestic manufacturers a price edge without cutting margins. It makes imports costlier, which can be used deliberately to fight deflation by pushing domestic prices up. And for a government carrying large local-currency debt, a weaker currency combined with rising nominal wages can quietly reduce the real burden of that debt over time.

body.text: A weaker currency is never free. It is a transfer: cheaper exports for your factories, in exchange for pricier imports for your citizens and your import-dependent industries. Every currency war is really an argument about who pays that bill, at home and among trading partners.

children.text: The Number That Matters More Than the Headline USD/INR Quote

markDefs.definition: An index that adjusts a currency's trade-weighted value against a basket of trading partner currencies for the inflation differential between countries, showing whether the currency has become more or less competitive in real terms.

children.text: A rupee that falls 5% against the dollar has not necessarily become 5% more competitive against India's actual trading partners. That is what the
real effective exchange rate

is built to answer. The RBI publishes REER indices against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, adjusted for the inflation gap between India and those partner economies. A country whose inflation runs consistently hotter than its trading partners can see its currency depreciate in nominal terms every year while its REER, and its real competitiveness, barely moves.

body.caption: A working approximation for how much of a nominal currency move survives as a real, REER-equivalent competitiveness gain

body.title: Nominal Move, Real Result
body.prompt: The rupee depreciates 5% against the US dollar over one year in nominal terms. Indian CPI inflation for the year runs at 7%, US CPI inflation at 2%. Using the approximation above, what is India's approximate real, REER-equivalent change over the year, in percentage points? Enter a negative number if the rupee actually became less competitive in real terms.
body.explanation: Real change ≈ 5% − (7% − 2%) = 5% − 5% = 0%. Despite a 5% nominal fall, India gained essentially no real competitiveness, because the higher domestic inflation ate up the entire nominal move. This is the trap policymakers watch for: a currency can look like it is devaluing while doing almost nothing for actual export competitiveness.

children.text: Case Study in Real Time: The August 2015 Yuan Shock

On 11 August 2015, the People's Bank of China cut the yuan's daily reference rate by roughly 1.9%, its largest single-day move in two decades, and followed up with further cuts over the next two days for a cumulative fall of close to 3% against the dollar. Chinese officials called it a technical reform to make the reference rate more market-driven. Global markets read it as the opening move of a fresh currency war, coming at a moment when Chinese growth was already slowing.

The fallout reached Dalal Street within two weeks. On 24 August 2015, since remembered on Indian financial media as a Black Monday, the Nifty fell by roughly 6% intraday and the Sensex shed more than 1,600 points, among the sharpest single-day falls either index had seen since the 2008 financial crisis. India had not changed. Its current account, its inflation trajectory and its growth outlook were essentially the same as the week before. What moved was fear that Beijing's devaluation was the start of a broader round of competitive devaluations across emerging markets.

body.title: Nifty 50 Through the August 2015 Yuan Shock (Approximate Closing Levels)

body.text: Notice what actually moved: not just Chinese assets. A reference-rate decision in Beijing wiped a meaningful chunk off Indian equity portfolios within two weeks, purely on fear that the move was the first shot in a broader currency war. That fear, not any change in India's own fundamentals, was what got priced into the Nifty that week.

children.text: The transmission channel to individual stocks was uneven, and worth noticing now because it recurs throughout this course. A weaker yuan does not directly help an Indian IT exporter's revenue, since that revenue is mostly dollar-denominated and China is not a major market for Indian IT services. But the rupee's own modest depreciation that week, itself partly a symptom of the same panic, gave IT majors a small tailwind on their dollar earnings when translated back into rupees. An investor scanning IT sector export exposure on screener.in that week would have found limited comfort either way: the bigger story was market-wide risk-off selling, not a sector-specific currency effect.

body.title: You Are Managing an EM Equity Book on 12 August 2015
body.scenario: You run an emerging-markets-focused equity book. On 11 August, the PBoC cut the yuan's daily reference rate by 1.9%. Overnight, Asian markets are falling and there is open talk on trading desks of a new currency war, with speculation that Vietnam, South Korea and others may respond by weakening their own currencies to protect export competitiveness. Your book is overweight Indian IT exporters and underweight domestic-consumption names.
body.prompt: What do you actually do to your positioning over the next 48 hours, and what would make you reverse course quickly?
body.modelAnswer: First, separate what has actually changed from what markets fear might change. China's growth outlook was already soft before 11 August, so the devaluation itself is a symptom, not a fresh shock to India's own fundamentals. Second, watch the PBoC's next two fixings closely: a third consecutive cut on 12 or 13 August would confirm this is a sustained policy move rather than a one-off technical adjustment, and that is the trigger to trim broad EM beta, not just Chinese exposure, since markets tend to sell emerging markets as a bloc during a currency war scare. Third, on the book itself: an overweight in Indian IT exporters is not a natural China-devaluation hedge, since their revenue exposure is US and Europe dominated, not China, so don't mistake that position for protection. A more direct response is checking whether the rupee is depreciating in sympathy, which would modestly help IT earnings in rupee terms but hurt domestic-consumption names facing costlier imported inputs. Reverse the defensive trim quickly if the PBoC stabilises the fixing within days and Nifty volatility (India VIX) drops back toward pre-11-August levels, since that would signal markets have concluded this was a one-off adjustment rather than the start of a currency war.

body.title: Currency War vs Currency Crisis: Don't Confuse the Two

columns.label: Currency War
points: Starts with a deliberate policy choice by a central bank
Other countries may retaliate by devaluing in response
The underlying economy is often functioning fine, this is a fight over competitiveness
Example: China, August 2015, and the broader 2010 currency war era covered later in this course

columns.label: Currency Crisis
points: Starts with a collapse in investor confidence, not a policy choice
The central bank is usually trying to defend the currency, not weaken it
The underlying economy typically has real vulnerabilities: thin reserves, high foreign debt
Example: Thailand, July 1997, and India's own 1991 balance of payments crisis

body.label: RBI's REER framework
body.context: Published monthly by the RBI, trade-weighted and inflation-adjusted, currently benchmarked to a 2015-16 base year. This is the number to track alongside the headline USD/INR quote, not instead of it.

cards.definition: A currency weakening due to market forces, with no deliberate policy action behind the move.
A central bank deliberately weakening its currency, through rate policy, intervention or announcement, for a competitive trade advantage.
A pattern where multiple countries treat exchange rates as competitive tools, devaluing or intervening in response to each other.
A trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted index showing whether a currency has become more or less competitive in real terms, distinct from the nominal exchange rate.
A disorderly currency collapse driven by a loss of investor confidence and capital flight, where the central bank loses control rather than choosing the move.

points: Depreciation, competitive devaluation and currency war describe three different mechanisms, not one sliding scale of the same thing.
Competitive devaluation requires a deliberate policy choice aimed at a competitive outcome; routine RBI intervention to smooth volatility is not that.
A weaker currency is a transfer, not a free lunch: cheaper exports for domestic producers, costlier imports for domestic consumers and import-dependent industries.
The real effective exchange rate, not the headline USD/INR quote, is what tells you whether a currency move has actually changed competitiveness.
China's August 2015 yuan reference-rate cut moved Indian equity markets sharply within two weeks despite no material change in India's own fundamentals, purely on currency war fear.
A currency crisis and a currency war look similar in headlines but run in opposite directions: one is imposed on a central bank, the other is chosen by one.
